Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Designing Low Emission Zones: Theory and Evidence
Nano Barahona, Natalia Fabra, Imelda, and Juan-Pablo Montero 
NBER Working Paper No. 36037
November 2026
JEL No. D12, H23, L98, Q53, R48
ABSTRACT
Low Emission Zones (LEZs), which exclude polluting vehicles from parts of a city, are spreading. 
Yet how their design affects welfare is poorly understood. Unlike price instruments, LEZs ration 
access inefficiently, imposing costs on inframarginal drivers of restricted vehicles. In our model, 
welfare is quasi-convex in LEZ size, yielding bang-bang principles: LEZs should be as large as 
possible or not implemented at all; cleaner vehicles (e.g., hybrids) could be exempt as transition 
technologies but later restricted, which may require planner commitment. Using new-car 
purchases, we find Madrid’s LEZ shifted buyers toward cleaner cars, but the surplus losses of 
switchers and inframarginal drivers exceeded emission savings.

1 Introduction
Road transport is a leading source of greenhouse gases and local air pollutants. The
associated health, economic, and societal consequences are substantial and well docu-
mented (OECD 2014; World Health Organization 2025). An increasingly popular policy
tool to handle these external costs is the creation of Low Emission Zones (LEZs): urban
areas that restrict access to vehicles that fail to meet certain environmental standards.
Introduced in 2008 in several German cities, LEZs are now found all over Europe and in
many cities around the world, including Shanghai, Beijing, Haifa, Seoul, and Jakarta.1
Even some U.S. cities have begun experimenting with more targeted versions of LEZs,
particularly for freight and last-mile delivery.
An often overlooked aspect of LEZs is the significant variation in their design, par-
ticularly concerning the geographic scope of the covered area and the types of restricted
vehicles. For example, the LEZ in Berlin, implemented in 2008, spans 88 km2, restricts
some, but not all, gasoline and diesel cars, and imposes different geographic restrictions
among its restricted cars. In contrast, the LEZ in Madrid, known as Madrid Central and
implemented a decade later, covers a much smaller area, of just 5 km2, but restricts all
gasoline and diesel cars, making no geographic distinction among them.
Such wide variation raises important policy-design questions, which motivate this
paper: What is the optimal LEZ size, and should some cars be restricted more, or later,
than others? A central goal of a LEZ is to achieve sustained reductions in air pollution
by creating incentives for drivers to switch to cleaner modes of transportation, whether
cleaner cars or public transit (Ayuntamiento de Madrid 2018, arts. 22–23, p. 139).2 Given
this goal, we show that the answers to the above questions follow a bang-bang logic: for
a welfare-maximizing planner, a LEZ should be either as large as politically feasible or
not implemented at all. Moreover, when less-polluting vehicles such as hybrids are to be
restricted, such a planner restricts them in the same way as other restricted cars, but
later.
Using Madrid’s LEZ as both motivation and evidence, we initiate our analysis by
assessing its impact on the adoption of hybrids and electric vehicles (EVs), which, along
with liquefied petroleum gas or compressed natural gas vehicles (LPG/CNG), are exempt
from the restriction. Looking at sales of new cars and comparing Madrid to other cities in
Spain, we estimate a synthetic difference-in-differences model (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021)
and show that Madrid’s LEZ was effective in accelerating the adoption of hybrids and

in Spain (Delgado-Lindeman et al. 2025).
2This goal is consistent with EU policy, under which LEZs are an important instrument for cities seeking to

over the period 2008–2016, find that LEZs reduced pollution but not congestion, which they attribute

2
LPG/CNG vehicles, and to a lesser extent EVs, while also reducing the sales of new
gasoline and diesel cars.
These findings raise policy questions that reach beyond Madrid’s LEZ design. Was it
welfare-improving to fully exempt LPG/CNG and hybrid cars? Two alternatives arise. A
spatial alternative would restrict these cars less stringently than gasoline and diesel cars—
barring them from a smaller zone, as in Berlin’s tiered design. A temporal alternative
would treat them as transition technologies: unrestricted for now, but with an announced
timetable under which they later face the same restrictions as gasoline and diesel cars.
Both alternatives would make EVs more attractive relative to them, but through different
channels, and at different costs to their current owners and to drivers thinking of switching
away from gasoline. So the natural question is: How do the two alternatives compare,
and when does either yield higher welfare than Madrid’s full exemption of LPG/CNG
and hybrids?
We shed light on these and related questions with a simple dynamic model of three
horizontally differentiated car types (gasoline, hybrids, EVs) that also differ in their emis-
sion rates. Hybrids—which represent any intermediate technology such as LPG/CNG—
pollute less than gasoline cars but more than EVs. The model formalizes the bang-bang
rationale: to maximize welfare, all restricted vehicles should be treated equally, and
the LEZ should be either as large as possible or not implemented at all if it falls be-
low a minimum scale. Within this rationale, hybrids may still qualify as a transition
technology—kept as unrestricted as EVs for some time, and then as restricted as gaso-
line cars. This transition-technology design, however, may require commitment from the
planner.
Unlike price-based instruments, such as taxes and tradable quotas, which operate
under an efficient rationing rule, LEZs operate under an inefficient (e.g., proportional)
rationing rule, leading to quasi-convex welfare functions.3 To see this, imagine a social
planner who introduces a small pollution tax on dirty vehicles. The welfare impact of this
tax is confined to the marginal drivers who switch to cleaner cars in response to the tax.
Importantly, social welfare is unaffected by the tax impact on inframarginal drivers—
those who do not switch. Initially, the welfare loss to switchers from moving away from
their preferred (i.e., no-intervention) car is smaller than the social welfare gain from
reduced emissions. The planner finds it optimal to increase the tax up to its Pigouvian
level, where the (concave) welfare function reaches its maximum level. Importantly, unless
set far above its Pigouvian level, a tax always increases social welfare, no matter how
small.4
Because LEZs involve inefficient rationing, they differ fundamentally from price-
based instruments; under some conditions, even the best LEZ may yield lower welfare
3See Tirole (1988) for more on rationing rules.
4Shadow costs of public funds may affect the optimal tax in either direction according to a Ramsey
formula but never eliminate it (Laffont and Tirole 1996).
3
than having no LEZ. To see this, consider a small LEZ that restricts only gasoline cars.
Unlike a tax, a LEZ imposes a welfare cost on every inframarginal driver who continues
driving gasoline cars. These individuals will have to change their transport mode (e.g.,
to public transit), reroute around the LEZ, or cancel trips altogether. If the number of
inframarginal individuals is large, the welfare losses borne by them can be large relative to
the net welfare gains from the few marginal individuals who switch from gasoline cars to
hybrids or EVs. As a result, a small LEZ may reduce welfare—unless it can be expanded
above a minimum scale, large enough to leave few inframarginal drivers restricted.
This minimum scale is the LEZ size that achieves the same welfare as the no-
intervention outcome. We show that when pollution harm is not too large, or substitution
toward cleaner cars is weak, the minimum scale may not exist, so implementing any LEZ
reduces welfare. In contrast, when pollution harm is relatively large, and substitution is
strong, the minimum scale can be small, even zero, meaning that almost any LEZ would
increase welfare in our model. Even then, the quasi-convexity of the welfare function
implies that welfare is highest at the largest possible LEZ.
This bang-bang logic—to reduce the number of inframarginal consumers of restricted
cars as much as possible—also explains why, in our model, all restricted cars should be
treated equally, i.e., subject to the largest politically feasible LEZ. We also show that, in
many cases, the planner maximizes welfare by treating hybrids as a transition technology:
initially exempt from the restrictions, but subject to them at a later stage. Anticipating
the declining value of hybrids, and provided the planner can commit to the announced
future restrictions, some individuals may choose to switch away from hybrids before
the restrictions take effect.5 Consequently, fewer hybrids remain in circulation by the
time the restriction arrives, reducing the cost of imposing it. In this sense, a LEZ with
a transition technology works more like a price-based instrument: it affects consumer
choices at the margin without destroying value for inframarginal consumers before the
restriction becomes active.6
We conduct an empirical evaluation of Madrid’s LEZ, focusing on new-car adoption
and welfare. Because car prices and preferences cannot be projected far ahead, we esti-
mate impacts around policy implementation and ask whether, at that time, the necessary
conditions for even considering a LEZ were met. That is, we ask whether there was a
minimum scale above which some LEZ design could improve welfare. We focus on house-
holds buying a new car, since that is where fleet composition changes: a second-hand
purchase mostly reallocates the existing stock. Our welfare estimates account for the
private costs of switching away from households’ preferred options, the utility loss borne
5Some switch to electric vehicles, while others move to gasoline cars; the latter case is less relevant, as
gasoline cars are already restricted.
6Our definition of a transition technology differs from alternative notions, which are often based on the
idea that electric vehicles remain too expensive or unfamiliar to serve as a viable outside option for many
gasoline drivers. Under that view, hybrids should remain unrestricted until these concerns dissipate.
While our definition is not in conflict with that view, it is fundamentally different.
4
by those who continue to buy restricted cars, and the lifetime externalities of the chosen
vehicles.
In the spirit of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995), we estimate demand for new cars
using registration data covering new cars sold in Spain from 2015 to 2019, together with
their prices and characteristics. Consumers’ preferences for cars, and their willingness to
pay to avoid the LEZ, vary with income and other consumer characteristics. Consistent
with our motivating evidence, we find that some consumers switch from gasoline and
diesel cars toward hybrids, LPG/CNG cars, and EVs. But the resulting externality
savings fall well short of the private losses: consumer surplus falls substantially more than
the reduction in externality costs. The private cost of tightening the restriction exceeds
the emission benefit throughout the range of intensities we evaluate, so a larger LEZ
would not have helped; nor would extending the restrictions to LPG/CNG vehicles and
hybrids, which raises the share of gasoline and diesel cars without materially increasing
EV adoption.
These negative results could be reversed under a LEZ design that also restricts
LPG/CNG and hybrids, if the following conditions are met: a substantially higher social
cost of emissions combined with a larger restricted zone, or stronger substitution toward
EVs. All this suggests that, at least in Madrid, the necessary conditions for considering a
LEZ in the first place were not satisfied. It also points to a broader conclusion: for a LEZ
to improve welfare, there must be fewer drivers buying gasoline and diesel cars, and the
barriers to adopting cleaner ones must be lower. For EVs, these barriers include limited
access to charging, short perceived driving range, and long charging times (Rosales-
Tristancho et al. 2022).
It is important to point out that these negative results abstract from any local
benefits that a LEZ may bring to residents and businesses within the restricted area,
such as safer streets and improved public space. This raises the broader question of
who ultimately determines LEZ design. This paper takes the stance of a planner who
cares about overall welfare. A narrower perspective is that of a decision maker who cares
mostly about the welfare of residents in the restricted area. A local constituency may
evaluate a small LEZ quite differently, and possibly quite favorably, than such a planner.
The wide variation in LEZ size that we observe—with Berlin and Madrid providing good
examples—may partly reflect these different perspectives. Our contribution should be
understood from the broader perspective: how best to use the LEZ instrument when the
objective is overall welfare.7
Our paper contributes to four strands of the literature. First, we contribute to
the vast literature on car markets. Closest to our work are the papers by Adda and
Cooper (2000) and Gillingham et al. (2022), which pay explicit attention to both new
and second-hand units and market dynamics. However, we depart from both papers in
7And in doing so, we completely abstract from the political-economy question of why cities opt for LEZs
as opposed to more efficient instruments.
5
important ways. Adda and Cooper (2000) consider a single type of car, abstracting from
any horizontal differentiation—both in preferences and pollution rates—which lies at the
core of our framework. Gillingham et al. (2022), by contrast, offer a rich framework with
various degrees of differentiation (in preferences and pollution) but, by focusing on sta-
tionary equilibria, abstract from aggregate shocks that may evolve over time and generate
transition dynamics. Unlike both papers, we study how a market with differentiated cars
adjusts over time to a LEZ. This adjustment matters for policy design, especially when
hybrids can be treated as a transition technology.8
Second, we contribute to the growing literature evaluating the performance of LEZ
programs around the world.9 Several papers document the positive health impacts of
LEZs, driven by reductions in local air pollution (e.g., Klauber et al. 2024; Beshir and
Fichera 2022; Margaryan 2021; Gehrsitz 2017), although these benefits come at the cost
of restricted mobility (Sarmiento, W¨agner, and Zaklan 2023). Others provide reduced-
form evidence on the effects of LEZs on traffic, finding reductions in congestion within the
restricted area (Galdon-Sanchez et al. 2023) that are often temporary, negative spillovers
to adjacent areas (Tassinari 2024), or simply no effects (Bernardo, Fageda, and Flores-
Fillol 2021; Garson et al. 2026).
Only a few papers study the effects of LEZs on the adoption of lower-emission
vehicles, which are central to the policy-design questions at the core of our analysis. An
early exception is Wolff (2014), who shows that German LEZs induced residents living
close to restricted areas to increase their adoption of low-emission vehicles. More recently,
also in the context of German LEZs, Aydin, Gehrsitz, and Traxler (2024) find that highly
polluting vehicles were replaced by cleaner gasoline cars.10 These empirical findings are
consistent with the theoretical model we develop in this paper, as well as with the evidence
on Madrid’s LEZ that motivates it. However, none of these papers evaluate whether the
effects of induced low-emission vehicle adoption are large enough to offset the welfare
costs associated with restricted mobility and distorted choices.
Third, we contribute to the extensive literature comparing the performance of dif-
ferent policy instruments, typically categorized as either price-based (e.g., taxes, tradable
quotas) or command-and-control (e.g., emissions and technology standards). While LEZs
clearly fall within the command-and-control (CAC) category, they differ from other in-
struments in this group due to the bang-bang rationale underlying their optimal design.
Under most standard CAC instruments, the “marginal-inframarginal” tradeoff at the

Relatedly, Almagro et al. (2024), Durrmeyer and Mart´ınez (2026), Ater et al. (2026),
and Cook and Li (2025) quantify the welfare effects of different urban-transportation
policies—road pricing, transit fares, and service frequencies in Chicago; tolls and license-

long-run margin: the adoption of lower-emission vehicles.
Finally, we contribute to the literature on time inconsistency in environmental pol-
icy, although through a distinctive channel: in our setting, the commitment problem
does not arise under taxes—it arises only under a LEZ design that involves transition
technologies. This stands in contrast with the standard framing (e.g., Laffont and Tirole
1996; Helm, Hepburn, and Mash 2003), where time inconsistency stems from the plan-
ner’s ex post incentive to renege on ex ante (optimal) regulatory commitments—whether
taxes or standards—once agents have invested in irreversible abatement technologies or
R&D. Ours does not follow this expropriation logic but, rather, a pure discounting one:
when hybrids are not so dirty, the initial announcement of their future restriction fails to
induce enough switching toward cleaner options to reduce the number of inframarginal
hybrid users sufficiently to justify restricting them ex post.12
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background
on Madrid Central, describes the data sources, and presents motivating evidence of its
impact on green vehicle adoption. Section 3 develops a dynamic model of car choice and
examines the implications for the optimal LEZ design. Section 4 presents the structural
estimation, and Section 5 conducts the counterfactual analysis. Section 6 concludes.
Additional results and proofs are relegated to the Appendix.

intensity λ, where ∆Ei(1) is driver i’s emission savings per displaced car at the current
intensity (Appendix F.1). This implies that, at any intensity, a euro of driver i’s private
cost buys at most αi ∆Ei(1)/(1 − ρ) euros of emission savings. Second, we show that,
at our estimates, this ceiling is below one euro for virtually all drivers (Appendix F.2).68
Condition (23) therefore holds at every λ ≥ 0, so welfare decreases with LEZ intensity
everywhere.

5.2 When could the LEZ work?
In this subsection, we explore conditions under which a LEZ could generate positive
welfare gains. We discuss two changes that could make a LEZ more effective: higher
externality damages and stronger substitution across cars.
5.2.1 Higher externality damages
We multiply externality damages by 4. Our estimates imply only a modest damage
gap between gasoline cars and hybrids, so the emission savings of the LEZ are small.
Higher damages increase the benefits of the LEZ. Because only the valuation of damages
changes, the three LEZ rows in Panel B of Table 6 have the same market shares as in
Panel A. At its current intensity, the welfare effect of the existing LEZ improves but
remains negative, while the stricter designs still do worse.
Panel (b) of Figure 8 considers a more intense LEZ. As our theory predicts, welfare is
quasi-convex in the LEZ’s intensity. With higher damages, the curve becomes U-shaped.
44
A tighter restriction initially destroys surplus faster than it generates emission savings,
but eventually the latter begins to dominate. A LEZ that only restricts gasoline and
diesel cars reaches its minimum near −e2.59 thousand at an intensity of about 3 times
the current intensity and then rises. The stricter design that also restricts hybrids crosses
zero only at roughly 11 times the current intensity. This threshold shows how unlikely
a LEZ is to generate welfare gains under Madrid’s conditions, even before counting the
losses imposed on owners of second-hand restricted cars.70
5.2.2 More price-elastic demand
The performance of a LEZ also depends on how much demand it displaces and on
how much surplus that displacement destroys. Both are governed by αi/(1 − ρ), which
sets the slope of the residual demand curve.71 We scale it by 4, raising the mean own-
price elasticity from −5.27 to −19.74, well outside the range previous studies report for
automobile markets. In particular, we scale both αi and ϕi by 4, so that willingness to
pay to avoid the LEZ, ϕi/αi, stays at its baseline estimate.72
Panel C of Table 6 reports the result. At the current intensity, all three LEZ designs
still deliver negative net benefits. Since ϕi/αi stays the same, a driver who keeps a
restricted car loses as much as in the baseline counterfactual. However, many more
drivers switch. At the estimated αi, the LEZ leaves most of the gasoline and diesel fleet
in place. At the scaled αi, the same LEZ removes most gasoline and diesel cars from the
fleet, yet the surplus those buyers give up is rather small.
Figure 8 sets the two exercises—higher externality damages and flatter demand—
side by side. In both, welfare first falls and then rises, consistent with the bang-bang logic
of Section 3. The design that also restricts hybrids eventually raises welfare in both, but
the exercises differ in how intense the LEZ must be. More serious damages make each
switch more valuable but leave substitution just as difficult, so this design raises welfare
only beyond 11 times the current intensity. Flatter demand makes substitution cheaper,
so the same design raises welfare at a much lower intensity.73

6 Conclusions
We have shown, both theoretically and empirically, that LEZs differ fundamentally
from price-based instruments (e.g., taxes, tradable quotas). A tax on polluting cars, no
matter how small, always increases social welfare by inducing drivers to switch toward
cleaner vehicles, unless, of course, it is set too far above its Pigouvian level. A LEZ that
restricts polluting cars, by contrast, may not be worth considering in the first place. It
must be stringent enough to induce substantial switching while leaving sufficiently few
inframarginal users affected by the restriction; otherwise, having no LEZ may yield higher
welfare. Our estimates suggest that this was the case for Madrid’s LEZ. Although the
policy shifted some buyers toward cleaner cars, the surplus losses it generated far exceeded
the gains from the emissions it saved. Our counterfactual analysis clarifies what it would
take for a LEZ in Madrid to be welfare-improving: LPG/CNG and hybrids would also
have to be restricted, externality damages would have to be much larger, or the residual
demand for polluting vehicles sufficiently flat to generate stronger substitution toward
cleaner alternatives.
These findings also speak to the role of combining LEZs with other instruments.
In Weitzman’s (1974) prices-versus-quantities framework, for example, combining instru-
ments may be optimal because the planner faces a friction: policy cannot be continuously
adjusted as new information arrives. That friction is absent from our framework. If price-
based instruments are available, there is no intrinsic reason to combine them with an
inefficient rationing instrument such as a LEZ, unless they cannot be set at their optimal
levels. In such a case, prices can play a supporting role by reducing the number of infra-
marginal users. By making polluting vehicles less attractive, or cleaner vehicles easier to
adopt, they may help satisfy the necessary conditions under which a LEZ becomes worth
considering.
While our focus in this paper has been strictly on a LEZ’s ability to induce drivers
to switch toward cleaner vehicles, it is important to recognize that such policies may also
generate local benefits for residents and businesses within the restricted area, including
improvements in urban amenities. To the extent that these benefits are quantitatively im-
portant, the relatively limited geographic scope of Madrid’s LEZ may have represented an
adequate way to strike a balance between local welfare gains and city-wide welfare losses
associated with restricting vehicle access. Quantifying this broader tradeoff, however, is
beyond the scope of this paper.
